chunks: How a flash ADC works. The question: How does a flash ADC work?
A flash ADC measures a voltage in one step by checking every possible level at the same time.
One comparator (a circuit that says whether one voltage is higher than another) sits at each level. Counting how many say "yes" gives the answer.
It is the fastest kind of ADC, but the number of comparators doubles with every extra bit.
Picture a tank with a row of float switches at evenly spaced heights. When the water rises, every switch below the water line trips, and every switch above it stays off.
To know the level, you just count the tripped switches. The input voltage is the water, and the comparators are the switches.
The weakness is the cost: a finer reading needs many more switches.
A 2-bit flash ADC. Three comparators (C3, C2, C1) compare V in with taps at 3/4, 1/2, 1/4 of V ref ; each tap goes to the inverting (minus ) input.
The input bus runs to all the non-inverting (+) inputs, and wires that cross without a dot are not connected. A priority encoder turns the thermometer code T3 T2 T1 into D1 D0.
ADC: ("How an ADC works"): a circuit that turns a voltage into a number. Comparator: a circuit whose output says whether its input is above a threshold voltage.
Resistor ladder: ("Voltage divider: draw, equation, derivation"): equal resistors in series that make evenly spaced voltages, one at each tap.
Thermometer code: the pattern of comparator outputs, a run of ones with zeros above, like mercury in a thermometer.
Encoder: logic that turns the thermometer code into an ordinary binary number.
A 3-bit flash ADC with a 3. 3 volts reference uses 8 equal resistors, which make 7 thresholds spaced 3. 3 / 8, about 0. 41 volts apart: 0. 41, 0. 83, 1. 24, 1. 65, 2. 06, 2.
48, 2. 89 volts. An input of 1. 9 volts is above the first four, so those four comparators output 1 and the other three output 0.
The encoder turns four ones into binary 100, which is 4. An 8-bit version would need 255 comparators. That is the whole idea.
"A flash ADC compares the input against every possible threshold at once. A resistor ladder makes 2 to the N-1 evenly spaced reference voltages, one comparator per threshold.
The comparators output a thermometer code, ones up to the input level, and an encoder turns that into binary.
It's the fastest ADC architecture, one comparator delay, but the comparator count, area and power double with each bit and offsets must be below an LSB, so it's limited to around 8 bits."
